weeks.title: Addition facts: counting on and doubles

spell.rule: Short vowels a, e, i, o, u in one-syllable words (flat, step, pick, frog, drum)

weeks.read: A short story your child can mostly read alone, plus a longer story you read aloud each evening.

days.ma: Write 0–10 on paper scraps. Flip two and add by counting on from the bigger number (7 + 3: start at 7, say 8, 9, 10). Do ten flips and tally the answers said within 3 seconds.
days.en: Read a short story together. Afterward ask one who, what, where, when, why and how question each, and have your child answer in a full sentence, e.g. 'The fox went to the river because he was thirsty.'

days.ma: Doubles: use fingers or pairs of socks to show 1 + 1 up to 10 + 10. Write the ten doubles facts in a list, read them aloud twice, then cover the answers and quiz.
days.en: Short vowel sort: write flat, step, pick, frog and drum as column headings. Say sled, chip, plum, cat, hot, bed, fun and sit; your child writes each under the word with the same vowel sound.

days.ma: Near doubles: if 6 + 6 = 12, then 6 + 7 is one more. Solve 5 + 6, 7 + 8, 8 + 9 and 4 + 5 by saying the double first, then check with dried pasta pieces.
days.en: Fluency: your child reads one page of the story aloud, you read it back with expression, then they read it a third time trying to sound like you. Which reading sounded best?

days.ma: Turnaround facts: show with two piles of pasta that 3 + 8 and 8 + 3 make the same total. List five facts and their turnarounds, always counting on from the bigger number.
days.en: Agree on three rules for family book talks (one person speaks at a time, look at the speaker, ask when you don't understand). Practice them in a five-minute talk about the story's best part.

days.ma: Friday check: 4 + 4, 9 + 2, 6 + 7, 3 + 8, 5 + 5, 8 + 9, 7 + 0, 2 + 9. Say each answer within 3 seconds; circle any that took longer to practice next week.
days.en: Dictation: read 'The frog sat on a flat log.' and 'He said it was fun.' Your child writes them, then checks capital letters, periods and the spellings of said and was.

weeks.title: Making ten and subtraction facts

spell.rule: Long vowels with silent e: a_e, i_e, o_e, u_e (cake, smile, rope, cube)

weeks.read: A story with a clear beginning, middle and end – a folktale or picture book from the library.

days.ma: Make ten: draw a ten-frame (two rows of five boxes). Put 8 pasta pieces in it and 5 outside. Move 2 in to fill it: 10 + 3 = 13, so 8 + 5 = 13. Repeat with 9 + 4, 7 + 6 and 9 + 7.
days.en: Read a story, then fold a sheet into three: Beginning, Middle, End. Your child draws one picture in each and tells you how the beginning introduced the characters and how the ending wrapped things up.

days.ma: Partners of ten: call out a number from 0 to 10 and your child answers with the partner that makes 10 (3 → 7). Then do partners of 20 with numbers from 10 to 20 (14 → 6).
days.en: Silent e: write cap, kit, hop, cub and plan. Add an e to each (cape, kite, hope, cube, plane) and read both words aloud. Talk about how the e makes the first vowel say its name.

days.ma: Think addition to subtract: for 13 – 8, ask '8 plus what makes 13?' Practice with 15 – 7, 12 – 9, 16 – 8 and 11 – 4, counting up on fingers if needed.
days.en: Small moment story: your child tells you about one thing that happened this summer, out loud, with a beginning, middle and end and what they saw, heard and felt. Then they write the first three sentences.

days.ma: Fact families: with 6, 9 and 15, write the four facts (6 + 9, 9 + 6, 15 – 6, 15 – 9). Then make fact families for 7, 8, 15 and for 5, 8, 13.
days.en: Finish the small moment story with a closing sentence about how it ended or how they felt. Check that every sentence starts with a capital and ends with a period.

days.ma: Friday check: 9 + 5, 8 + 6, 7 + 7, 14 – 6, 17 – 9, 12 – 5, 10 – 3, 13 – 4. Your child explains the make-ten or think-addition step for two of them.
days.en: Dictation: 'They rode a bike to the lake.' and 'There is a cake on the plate.' Check the silent e words and the periods, then your child reads their story to someone.

weeks.title: Odd and even numbers

spell.rule: Short or long? Word pairs where a silent e changes the vowel (tap/tape, kit/kite, hop/hope, cub/cube)

weeks.read: A story where a character faces a big problem – talk about how they feel and what they do.

days.ma: Pairs test: grab a handful of pasta (up to 20) and line the pieces up in pairs. If every piece has a partner the number is even; if one is left over it is odd. Record five handfuls in a two-column table.
days.en: Read a story and stop at the big problem. Ask 'How does the character feel? What will they do?' After finishing, compare: did they respond the way your child guessed?

days.ma: Count by 2s from 0 to 20 while hopping, then from 1 to 19. Write both lists and notice the last digit of every even number (0, 2, 4, 6, 8).
days.en: Collective nouns: match group words to things – a flock of birds, a team of players, a herd of cows, a bunch of grapes, a pack of wolves. Your child says a sentence using each one.

days.ma: Doubles make evens: write each even number to 20 as two equal addends (10 = 5 + 5, 14 = 7 + 7). Use pairs of socks to check 16 and 18.
days.en: Write tap, tape, kit, kite, hop, hope, cub and cube on cards. Your child sorts them into short and long vowel piles, reads each one, then uses one pair in a single sentence.

days.ma: Odd or even hunt: count things around the house – chairs, windows, stairs, forks in the drawer. Predict odd or even first, then pair them up to check.
days.en: Your child writes about a time they faced a challenge (a first day, a lost toy): how they felt at first and what they did. Read it aloud together and add one detail where you ask 'What happened next?'

days.ma: Friday check: Is 13 odd or even? 18? 7? Write 12 and 20 as doubles. Can 15 crackers be shared equally between two people? Your child explains how they know.
days.en: Dictation: 'Could you fly a kite near a flock of birds?' and 'I would hope so.' Check the question mark, the capital I and the long and short vowel words.

weeks.title: Word problems within 20

spell.rule: Long a spelled ai and ay: ai in the middle of a word, ay at the end (rain, paint, day, play)

weeks.read: A nonfiction book about an animal – look at the pictures first and guess what you'll learn.

days.ma: Act out problems with toys: '9 cars are in a box. 4 more are added. How many now?' Then 'Some cars were in a box. 5 more came and now there are 12. How many were there at first?' Write ☐ + 5 = 12.
days.en: Read a nonfiction animal book. Ask: What does it eat? Where does it live? How does it stay safe? Your child finds the page that answers each question.

days.ma: Compare problems: 'You have 14 grapes and I have 9. How many more do you have?' Line up two rows of pasta to see the difference, then solve two more like it.
days.en: Main topic: read one section. Your child says in one sentence what the whole section is about, then what one paragraph inside it focuses on.

days.ma: Bar drawing: draw a long bar for the total and split it into two parts. Use it for 'There are 17 birds. 8 fly away. How many are left?' and '6 red apples and some green apples make 15.'
days.en: ai or ay? Write rain, paint, train, mail, day, play, stay and gray. Your child sorts them, notices that ay comes at the end, then adds one more word to each group.

days.ma: Your child makes up a word problem about the kitchen (spoons, eggs, cups) for you to solve aloud, then you swap. Write the equation for each, using ☐ for the unknown.
days.en: Fact writing: your child writes three facts about the animal as full sentences, with a heading and a closing sentence such as 'Owls are amazing night hunters.'

days.ma: Friday check: three word problems – one adding to, one taking from, one comparing – each with an equation using ☐. Your child draws a picture or bar for one of them.
days.en: Dictation: 'The train was late because of the rain.' and 'Can we play all day?' Check the ai and ay words, the question mark and the spelling of because.

weeks.title: Place value: hundreds, tens and ones

spell.rule: Long e spelled ee and ea (seed, sleep, beach, team)

weeks.read: A nonfiction book with headings, bold words and a glossary – about space, weather or the human body.

days.ma: Bundle it: count 100 pasta pieces or paper clips into piles of ten. Ten tens make one hundred. Show 1 hundred, 3 tens and 4 ones and say the number: 134.
days.en: Text feature tour: in a nonfiction book find the table of contents, a heading, a caption, a bold word and the glossary. Your child explains what each one is for.

days.ma: Quick draw: you say 253; your child draws 2 hundred squares, 5 ten sticks and 3 ones dots. Then draw 407 and 360 and talk about what each zero means.
days.en: Glossary detective: pick two bold words. Your child guesses their meaning from the sentence around them, then checks the glossary. Were the guesses right?

days.ma: What's it worth? Write 528 and point at each digit: the 5 means 5 hundreds or 500, the 2 means 2 tens or 20, the 8 means 8 ones. Then do 706 and 870.
days.en: Long e sort: write seed, green, sleep, tree, seat, beach, team and read. Sort them into ee and ea lists and read each list fast. Add one more word to each.

days.ma: Trade game: draw 9 ten sticks and add one more. Ten tens make 1 hundred, so swap them for a square. Then show that 300 is 3 hundreds, 0 tens and 0 ones, or 30 tens.
days.en: Make a mini fact page about one thing from the book: a heading, three fact sentences, one word in bold (traced over darkly) and a one-line glossary at the bottom explaining it.

days.ma: Friday check: What is the 4 worth in 342? Draw 615. Write the number with 7 hundreds, 0 tens and 9 ones. How many tens make 100? How many hundreds are in 800?
days.en: Dictation: 'People sleep in the green tent by the beach.' and 'Read me a very good book.' Then your child reads you their fact page and you ask one question to find out more.

weeks.title: Counting and skip-counting to 1,000

spell.rule: Long o spelled oa, ow and oe (boat, snow, toe)

weeks.read: Fables – short animal stories with a lesson at the end. Read one each day.

days.ma: Skip-count by 10s from 0 to 200 while clapping, then start at 30, then at 45 (45, 55, 65 …). Write the 45 list up to 145.
days.en: Read a fable. Your child retells it in four sentences using first, next, then and last, and says the lesson in their own words.

days.ma: Count by 5s using nickels or tally marks: 5, 10, 15 … 100. Then keep going from 100 to 200. What digits do the numbers always end in?
days.en: Irregular past tense: change sit, hide, tell, run, go and see into the past (sat, hid, told, ran, went, saw). Use three of them to retell yesterday's fable.

days.ma: Count by 100s: 100, 200 … 1,000. Then start at 50 (50, 150, 250 …) and at 23 (23, 123, 223 …). Which digit changes each time?
days.en: Read a new fable aloud three times – once to learn the words, once more smoothly, once with voices for the animals. Your child picks the best version to read to someone.

days.ma: Count across a hundred: count by ones from 96 to 112, from 387 to 405 and from 695 to 710. Write the tricky part where the hundreds digit changes.
days.en: Your child writes a new ending for one fable: what if the character had made a different choice? Three to five sentences, ending with a new lesson.

days.ma: Friday check: count by 5s from 35 to 85; by 10s from 470 to 560; by 100s from 200 to 1,000; fill in 298, 299, ☐, ☐, 302.
days.en: Dictation: 'Does the snow show on the road?' and 'The goat only goes by boat.' Then your child tells the lesson of their favorite fable this week.

weeks.title: Reading and writing numbers to 1,000

spell.rule: Long i spelled igh, y and ie (night, fly, pie)

weeks.read: A poetry collection – read two or three poems each day and choose a favorite to learn.

days.ma: Number names: write one to nineteen, then twenty, thirty … ninety and hundred on paper scraps. Build 'three hundred forty-two' from the cards and write it in numerals.
days.en: Read three rhyming poems aloud. Your child claps the beat, then finds the rhyming pairs and any repeated lines. Talk about how the beat makes the poem fun to say.

days.ma: Expanded form: write 586 as 500 + 80 + 6. Do 349, 702 and 960. Then go backward: 400 + 70 + 3 = ?
days.en: Alliteration: find a line in a poem where several words start with the same sound. Make up your own, e.g. 'Silly snakes slide slowly', then two more about family pets or foods.

days.ma: Three ways: you say a number (such as 815); your child writes it in numerals, in words and in expanded form. Do four numbers, including one with a zero in the tens.
days.en: Shades of meaning: write walk, stroll, march, stomp and tiptoe on cards. Act each one out and line them up from quietest to loudest. Use one in a sentence.

days.ma: Hide-and-seek numbers: write ten three-digit numbers in words on scraps and hide them around a room. Your child finds each one and writes it in numerals beside it.
days.en: Learn four lines of a favorite poem by heart. Record it on a phone or tablet with expression, play it back, decide what to improve and record it again.

days.ma: Friday check: write 'six hundred nine' in numerals; write 473 in words and in expanded form; what is 300 + 5? What is 900 + 40 + 1?
days.en: Dictation: 'The light was high in the night sky.' and 'I will try again at four.' Then your child performs their poem for the family.

weeks.title: Consolidation: facts, odd and even, place value

spell.rule: Review: short vowels, silent e and the vowel teams ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, ow, igh

weeks.read: Re-read a favorite book from the last seven weeks and choose a page to perform aloud.

days.ma: Fact sprint: write 20 mixed addition and subtraction facts within 20. Your child answers them all, then tries the missed ones again a second time.
days.en: Re-read a favorite story. Your child sums it up in three sentences, then gives it a rating out of five and one reason for the rating.

days.ma: Odd or even totals: pick two number cards (0–9) and add them. Is the total odd or even? Prove it by pairing pasta. Play six rounds and look for a pattern.
days.en: Spelling review game: you say a word from the past seven weeks; your child spells it aloud and names the rule or vowel team (silent e, ai, ee …).

days.ma: Draw 365, 506 and 740 as hundred squares, ten sticks and ones dots. Write each one in words and in expanded form.
days.en: Edit a story written earlier this fall: add one detail, fix two spellings and check that every sentence starts with a capital and ends with punctuation.

days.ma: Skip-counting chain: count by 10s from 250 to 350, by 100s back down to 50, then by 5s from 50 to 100.
days.en: Your child tells a family member about the best thing they did this month, speaking clearly in full sentences and including who, where and one good detail.

days.ma: Friday check: 8 + 7, 16 – 9, 6 + 6, 13 – 5. Is 17 odd or even? Write 452 in expanded form and in words. Count by 100s from 140 to 640.
days.en: Dictation: 'Because it was a sunny day, we went to the beach.' and 'They said the coat was in the snow.' Check every review spelling and the comma.

weeks.title: Comparing numbers; 10 and 100 more or less

spell.rule: Compound words: two small words join to make a new word (sun + shine = sunshine)

weeks.read: A how-to book or kids' craft book – look at the numbered steps and the diagrams.

days.ma: Greater or less: write 462 and 426. Compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones, and write 462 > 426. Do five more pairs, including 709 and 790.
days.en: Read a how-to text (a recipe, craft or game rules). Talk about why the steps are numbered and what would happen if you skipped step 2.

days.ma: Alligator mouth: draw < and > as a hungry mouth that opens toward the bigger number. Compare 318 and 381, 504 and 540, 999 and 1,000, 250 and 205.
days.en: Diagrams: look at a picture or diagram in the how-to text. Your child explains what it shows that the words don't, e.g. which way to fold the paper.

days.ma: 10 more, 10 less: start at 450 and say 10 more and 10 less (460, 440). Then do 723, 108 and 395 – watch the jump to 405.
days.en: Cut word cards for sun, shine, rain, bow, bed, room, back, pack, cup and cake. Join them into compound words and use the two parts to explain each meaning.

days.ma: 100 more, 100 less: on a number path drawn on paper, jump 100 forward and back from 237. Do the same from 812, 150 and 904. Which digit changes?
days.en: Write instructions for a simple job – making a sandwich or brushing teeth – with a title, a 'You need' list and four numbered steps. Add a small labeled drawing for one step.

days.ma: Friday check: put >, < or = between 547 and 574, 830 and 803, 600 and 6 hundreds. What is 10 more than 395? 100 less than 702? 10 less than 900?
days.en: Dictation: 'On my birthday I got a cupcake and a new backpack.' and 'Is there something in the mailbox?' Check the compound words and the question mark.

weeks.title: Adding within 100

spell.rule: R-controlled vowels ar and or (car, park, horn, storm)

weeks.read: A picture book where a character has a strong opinion – something they love or can't stand.

days.ma: Tens and ones: for 34 + 25 add the tens (30 + 20 = 50), then the ones (4 + 5 = 9), so 59. Draw ten sticks and ones dots to check. Do 42 + 36 and 51 + 27.
days.en: Read a picture book about a character with a strong opinion. Ask who, what, where, when, why and how questions, then ask 'Do you agree with the character? Why?'

days.ma: Number line: draw an empty line. Solve 47 + 30 with three jumps of 10. Then 47 + 35: jump 30, then 5. Do 26 + 48 the same way.
days.en: ar or or? Write car, star, park, farm, horn, corn, storm and short. Your child sorts and reads them, then writes a sentence using two of each.

days.ma: Make a ten: 38 + 7 – take 2 from the 7 to make 40, then 40 + 5 = 45. Try 58 + 6, 29 + 14 and 67 + 25.
days.en: Opinion words: put like, love, adore, dislike and can't stand in order from strongest to weakest feeling. Use two of them in sentences about foods.

days.ma: Regroup: for 46 + 28 draw 4 tens 6 ones and 2 tens 8 ones. The 14 ones become 1 ten and 4 ones: 74. Do 37 + 45 and 59 + 33.
days.en: Write an opinion: 'The best season is … because …'. Include the opinion, two reasons joined with because and also, and a closing sentence.

days.ma: Friday check: 53 + 24, 36 + 9, 48 + 27, 65 + 30. Show one on a number line and explain the steps for another out loud.
days.en: Dictation: 'Your car is in the park.' and 'The storm was short.' Then your child reads the opinion piece to a family member, who asks a question and adds their own view.

weeks.title: Subtracting within 100

spell.rule: R-controlled er, ir and ur all make the same sound (her, bird, turn)

weeks.read: A nonfiction article or book that tries to convince you – why we should save water, recycle or plant trees.

days.ma: Subtract tens: for 85 – 30 count back by tens on a number line (75, 65, 55). Then 85 – 34: back 30, then back 4. Do 72 – 41.
days.en: Read a convincing text. Your child finds the author's main point and two reasons the author gives for it. Are they good reasons?

days.ma: Regroup: 52 – 27. Draw 5 tens 2 ones. You can't take 7 ones from 2, so break a ten into 10 ones (4 tens, 12 ones). Take away 2 tens 7 ones: 25. Do 63 – 38.
days.en: Write her, fern, bird, girl, first, turn, nurse and burn. Your child reads them all and notices they share one sound. Make a silly sentence with one word for each spelling.

days.ma: Count up to subtract: 71 – 46. Start at 46, jump 4 to 50, 20 to 70, 1 to 71 – a total jump of 25. Try 83 – 57 and 90 – 64.
days.en: Plan an opinion piece on a topic your child cares about (best pet, best game): the opinion and three reasons, each linked with because, also or and.

days.ma: Explain it: solve 64 – 29 two ways (regrouping and counting up). Your child explains why both give 35, then checks by adding 35 + 29.
days.en: Write and revise the opinion piece: add a describing word you have read or heard this week ('enormous', 'gently'), a closing sentence, and fix two spellings together.

days.ma: Friday check: 78 – 35, 60 – 24, 91 – 46, 50 – 8. Check one by adding. Explain why 40 – 19 gives the same answer as 41 – 20.
days.en: Dictation: 'The bird was the first to turn and fly.' and 'Were her ferns green?' Then your child reads their finished opinion piece aloud.

weeks.title: Adding three and four numbers

spell.rule: Diphthongs ou and ow (out, cloud, cow, town); ow often comes at the end of a word

weeks.read: A nonfiction book about harvest time, farming or how food gets to the table.

days.ma: Add three numbers: 23 + 15 + 7. Look for a friendly pair first (23 + 7 = 30), then add 15 to get 45. Do 16 + 24 + 18 and 35 + 12 + 5.
days.en: Read about how food gets from a farm to the table. Your child tells the steps in order and explains how each step leads to the next.

days.ma: Sock toss: label four bowls 10, 15, 20 and 25. Your child throws four rolled-up socks and adds the four scores. Play three rounds and compare totals.
days.en: Capitals for holidays and places: write Thanksgiving, Fourth of July, your town and your state. Your child fixes 'we visit our cousins in ohio on thanksgiving.'

days.ma: Column addition: write 34 + 21 + 12 + 18 in a column. Add the ones (15), write 5 and carry 1 ten, then add the tens: 85. Do 26 + 13 + 31 + 17.
days.en: Write out, house, cloud, round, cow, town, brown and clown. Your child sorts them into ou and ow and writes one sentence using three of the words.

days.ma: Explain why order doesn't matter: add 18 + 25 + 12 left to right, then by making 30 first. Your child says which way was easier and why it gives the same total.
days.en: Question and answer: your child picks a question ('Where do potatoes grow?'). Find the answer together in a book or by remembering a trip to a farm or store, and write it as a sentence.
Dictation: 'Our town has a parade on Thanksgiving.' and 'Many brown cows are out by the house.' Check the capital for the holiday and the ou and ow words.

weeks.title: Two-step word problems

spell.rule: Diphthongs oi and oy (coin, boil, boy, enjoy); oy usually comes at the end of a word

weeks.read: Letters and postcards in a story or book – notice how a letter starts and ends.

days.ma: Two steps: 'There were 45 apples. We ate 12, then picked 20 more. How many now?' Draw a bar for each step and write two equations.
days.en: Letter layout: look at a letter, card or note together. Point out the greeting (Dear …,), the body, the closing (Love, / Your friend,) and the commas after each.

days.ma: Start unknown: 'Some birds were on a fence. 17 flew away and 28 were left. How many were there at first?' Write ☐ – 17 = 28 and solve by adding.
days.en: oi or oy? Sort coin, point, boil, soil, boy, toy, joy and enjoy. Then use the rule to spell noise, join and annoy.

days.ma: Compare in two steps: 'You have 36 stickers and I have 19. If I get 10 more, who has more, and by how much?' Draw two bars to compare.
days.en: Formal or informal: compare 'Hey! Thanks for the toy!' with 'Thank you very much for the kind gift.' Who would each one be said to? Your child writes one sentence for a teacher and one for a friend.

days.ma: Your child writes a two-step problem about the family (shoes, plates, books) and solves it with equations. Then you solve it too to check.
days.en: Write a thank-you letter to a relative or neighbor: greeting, three complete sentences, closing and signature. Read it back and fix commas and capitals.

days.ma: Friday check: a two-step adding problem, one with the start unknown and a compare problem. Write an equation with ☐ for each.
days.en: Dictation as a mini letter: 'Dear Grandma,' then 'Thank you for the shiny coin.' then 'Your friend,'. Check the commas after the greeting and closing, then deliver the thank-you letter.

weeks.title: Money: counting coins

spell.rule: Contractions: an apostrophe shows where letters are left out (can't, it's, we'll)

weeks.read: A story with lots of conversation – read the characters' words in different voices.

days.ma: Coin sort: gather coins from a purse or jar. Name the penny (1¢), nickel (5¢), dime (10¢) and quarter (25¢). Sort them and count each pile by skip-counting.
days.en: Read a story with dialogue. Your child reads one character's lines and you read another's, in a different voice for each. Talk about how each sees the problem differently.

days.ma: Count mixed coins starting with the biggest: 1 quarter, 2 dimes, 1 nickel, 3 pennies → 25, 35, 45, 50, 51, 52, 53 = 53¢. Count four more handfuls.
days.en: Contractions: write do not, can not, is not, did not, I am, it is, we will and you are. Your child writes each contraction with the apostrophe where the letters were taken out.

days.ma: Same amount, different coins: make 30¢ three ways (3 dimes; 1 quarter and 1 nickel; 6 nickels). Then make 45¢ two ways.
days.en: Pick two characters from the story. How does each respond to the main problem? Your child completes 'At first ___ felt … but then …' for each one.

days.ma: Pretend store: label five household items with prices up to 99¢. Your child pays the exact amount with real coins and writes each price with the ¢ sign.
days.en: Readers' theater: practice a page of dialogue three times, then perform it for the family with different voices and expression.

days.ma: Friday check: count 2 quarters, 1 dime and 4 pennies; show 67¢ with the fewest coins; which is more, 3 dimes or 7 nickels? Write each amount with ¢.
days.en: Dictation: 'I'm sure it's not the right way.' and 'We'll go if you're ready, but don't be late.' Check every apostrophe.

weeks.title: Money: dollars, cents and word problems

spell.rule: Adding -s, -es, -ed and -ing with no change to the base word (jumps, boxes, played, helping)

weeks.read: A picture book with detailed illustrations – look for clues in the pictures that the words don't tell you.

days.ma: Dollars and cents: a dollar is 100¢. Count 4 quarters to make $1.00. Show $1.35 with a dollar bill (or a paper one) and coins, and write it with the $ sign and a decimal point.
days.en: Picture walk: before reading, look at the illustrations and predict what happens. Afterward, find a picture that shows a feeling or the setting better than the words do.

days.ma: Word problem: 'You have 2 dimes and 3 pennies. Grandpa gives you a quarter. How many cents do you have now?' Solve with coins, then write an equation.
days.en: Adjective or adverb? Adjectives describe nouns (a loud dog); adverbs describe verbs (the dog barked loudly). Sort quick/quickly, soft/softly, happy/happily and use one of each in a sentence.

days.ma: Toy store: draw three toys priced 35¢, 48¢ and 60¢. 'Which two can you buy with 90¢? How much is left?' Try all the pairs.
days.en: Endings: add -s or -es, -ed and -ing to jump, box, wish, play, help, fix and rest. Notice that -es goes after x, sh, ch and s.

days.ma: Change: 'A pencil costs 65¢ and you pay with a dollar. What is your change?' Count up from 65¢ to $1.00 with coins. Then do prices of 40¢ and 85¢.
days.en: Write a short story about a shopping trip (real or made up) using first, next, then and finally. Use two adjectives and two adverbs to describe actions and feelings.

days.ma: Friday check: show $1.25 with a dollar and a quarter; 3 dimes + 2 nickels + 4 pennies = ?¢; you have 75¢ and spend 38¢ – how much is left?
days.en: Dictation: 'Who fixed the boxes so quickly?' and 'She jumped and played happily.' Check the -ed endings and the adverbs.

weeks.title: Consolidation: adding, subtracting and money

spell.rule: Review: ar, or, er, ir, ur; ou, ow, oi, oy; contractions and compound words

weeks.read: A collection of winter stories read aloud before bed.

days.ma: Mixed practice: 47 + 38, 26 + 19 + 14, 93 – 57, 70 – 26. Your child chooses a strategy for each and explains it.
days.en: Choose a story written this fall. Read it together and pick one part to make better: more detail, stronger time words or a better ending.

days.ma: Money review: count a handful of coins and write the amount with ¢. Then make the same amount with fewer coins.
days.en: Publish the story: type it on a computer or tablet (or copy it in best handwriting) and add a title. Show your child how to fix a typo with the delete key.

days.ma: Order six three-digit numbers written on scraps from least to greatest, then write two comparisons with < or >.
days.en: Spelling relay: you say a review word; your child writes it and circles the vowel pattern (ar, or, er, ir, ur, ou, ow, oi, oy).

days.ma: Gift problem: 'A card costs 45¢ and a sticker costs 30¢. You have 85¢. Can you buy both? What is left?' Then your child makes one up with three items.
days.en: Add two pictures to the published story. Your child reads it aloud to the family, loudly and clearly enough for everyone to hear, and answers their questions.

days.ma: Friday check: 56 + 27; 81 – 45; 12 + 18 + 25 + 30; 4 quarters and 3 dimes = $?; compare 615 and 651; one two-step word problem.
days.en: Dictation: 'Don't turn the star around.' and 'My friend found a coin on my birthday.' Then read favorite pieces of this term's writing aloud to celebrate.

weeks.title: Telling time to five minutes

spell.rule: Two sounds of oo: moon and food, book and foot

weeks.read: Two versions of the same folktale from different cultures, such as a Cinderella-type tale from two countries.

days.ma: Make a clock from a paper plate or a drawn circle, with 1–12 and two hands. Show 3:00, 7:30 and 11:00. Which hand is longer, and what does each one show?
days.en: Read one version of a folktale from the library. Your child retells it and says what lesson it teaches.

days.ma: Count by 5s around the clock: each number is 5 more minutes (1 = 5, 2 = 10 … 12 = 60). Write the minutes outside each number on your clock.
days.en: Read a second version of the tale from a different culture. Make a two-column chart of what is the same and what is different (characters, setting, helper, ending).

days.ma: Five-minute times: show 4:15, 9:35, 2:50 and 6:05 on the paper clock. Read a real clock in the house three times today and write the time.
days.en: oo sort: write moon, food, spoon, school, book, look, foot and wood. Your child reads each and sorts them by sound (oo as in moon, oo as in book).

days.ma: Digital to analog: write 8:25, 12:40 and 3:55 like a digital clock. Your child shows each one on the paper clock, then makes times for you to read.
days.en: Talk about which version your child liked better. Take turns, listen all the way through, then build on each other: 'I agree because …' or 'I see it differently because …'

days.ma: Friday check: draw hands for 10:20, 5:45 and 1:05. Read three times you set on the clock. How many minutes are there from 3:00 to 3:25?
days.en: Dictation: 'Look at the moon from the school.' and 'You should put the book on the wood shelf.' Then your child names one way the two tales were alike.

weeks.title: Time: a.m., p.m. and the daily schedule

spell.rule: The oo sound spelled ew, ue and u_e (new, blue, flute)

weeks.read: A science book about the water cycle, the seasons or weather, with diagrams.

days.ma: a.m. is from midnight to noon, p.m. is from noon to midnight. List daily events (breakfast, lunch, bedtime, school starts, dinner) and write a time for each with a.m. or p.m.
days.en: Read about the water cycle or weather. Look at a diagram together and your child explains what the arrows show and how it helps make sense of the words.

days.ma: Day schedule: make a timeline of a weekend day with six events, each with a time to the nearest 5 minutes. Draw a clock face for two of them.
days.en: Science words: find three topic words (evaporate, cloud, temperature). Your child uses the sentence and the pictures to explain what each one means.

days.ma: Clock watch: pick three times to check the clock today (around 10:35 a.m., 2:50 p.m. and 6:15 p.m.). Your child reads the analog clock and writes the exact time with a.m. or p.m.
days.en: ew, ue, u_e: write new, grew, chew, blue, true, glue, flute and tune. They all make the same sound. Your child writes a sentence using one word of each spelling.

days.ma: Time in words: match 'seven thirty in the morning' to 7:30 a.m., 'quarter after four in the afternoon' to 4:15 p.m., and make up three more for each other to write.
days.en: Explain the process: your child draws the diagram from memory and writes three sentences explaining how one step leads to the next, using first, then and finally, plus a closing sentence.

days.ma: Friday check: show 7:45 a.m. and 4:10 p.m. on the paper clock; read three clocks you set; is dinner usually a.m. or p.m.? Write 'eight twenty-five at night' in digits.
days.en: Dictation: 'The blue cloud grew and grew.' and 'It is true that we need two cups of water.' Then your child explains the diagram to another family member.

weeks.title: Measuring in inches and feet

spell.rule: Soft c and soft g: c says /s/ and g says /j/ before e, i or y; dge after a short vowel (city, cage, badge)

weeks.read: Two or three nonfiction books about one animal, for a family research project.

days.ma: Inch hunt: use a ruler or tape measure. Measure a spoon, a crayon and a book in inches. Line the object up with 0, not with the end of the ruler!
days.en: Start a shared research project: choose an animal together and read a nonfiction book about it. What does the author want to explain? Write three questions you want answered.

days.ma: 12 inches make 1 foot. Find three things about 1 foot long. Then estimate how many feet long a table, a bed and a hallway are, and measure to check.
days.en: Use the table of contents and the index to find answers to your questions. Your child writes each fact on its own scrap of paper.

days.ma: Estimate first: guess the length of a TV remote, a shoe and a door in inches or feet. Write the guesses, measure, and talk about which were close.
days.en: Soft c and g: sort city, face, nice, cage, page, gem, badge and bridge. Notice dge comes right after a short vowel (badge, bridge) and ge after a long one (cage, page).

days.ma: Choose a tool: ruler, yardstick or tape measure? Decide which is best for a pencil, a couch and around your child's head, then measure each with that tool.
days.en: Read a second source on the same animal (another book or a children's science website with an adult). Add new facts to the scraps and answer one more who, what, where or why question.

days.ma: Friday check: measure a pencil and a fork in inches; estimate a table in feet, then measure; which tool for a hallway? How many inches are in a foot?
days.en: Dictation: 'Once I saw a nice cat in the city.' and 'Put the badge on page two.' Then your child shares the three best facts found so far.

weeks.title: Centimeters and meters; measuring with different units

spell.rule: Adding -ed and -ing: double the last letter after a short vowel (hop → hopping); drop the silent e (hope → hoping)

weeks.read: The research books from last week, plus a short article on the same animal to compare.

days.ma: Centimeters: find the cm edge of the ruler. Measure a paper clip, a key and a spoon in centimeters. Is a centimeter longer or shorter than an inch?
days.en: Compare two texts: write the two most important points each source gives about the animal. Which points are in both? Which appear in only one?

days.ma: Meters: a meter is 100 cm, about one big grown-up step. Mark 1 meter on the floor with string or tape. Estimate, then measure, a couch and a room in meters.
days.en: Sort the research facts into groups: looks like, eats, lives, babies. Each group becomes one section of the report.

days.ma: Measure twice: measure a book in inches and then in centimeters. Which number is bigger? Talk about why: smaller units mean you need more of them.
days.en: Write the report: a title, an opening sentence that names the animal, a short section for each group of facts and a closing sentence.

days.ma: Spoons and paper clips: measure a table edge in spoon lengths, then in paper clips. Which needed more? Connect this to inches and centimeters.
days.en: Doubling rule: run → running, stop → stopped, sit → sitting; hope → hoping, make → making, smile → smiled. Your child adds -ed or -ing to hop, bake, skip and ride.

days.ma: Friday check: measure a book in cm and in inches and explain which number is bigger and why; estimate a door in meters; how many centimeters make a meter?
days.en: Dictation: 'We were hopping and running.' Then type the report on a computer or tablet with your help, adding a heading and a picture or drawing.

weeks.title: Comparing lengths and length word problems

spell.rule: Prefixes un- (not, the opposite) and re- (again): unhappy, unlock, redo, retell

weeks.read: A story with a clear problem and solution – notice how the ending ties everything up.

days.ma: How much longer? Measure two pencils in centimeters. Line them up, find the difference and write it, e.g. 15 cm – 9 cm = 6 cm. Do the same with two spoons.
days.en: Read a story. Your child tells how the beginning sets up the problem and how the ending solves it. Ask a why question about the middle.

days.ma: Ruler number line: draw a line from 0 to 20 with equal spaces. Show 8 + 7 as two jumps forward and 18 – 6 as a jump back.
days.en: Prefixes: add un- or re- to happy, lock, kind, do, tell, read and fill. Your child explains each new meaning: un- means not or the opposite, re- means again.

days.ma: Length problems: 'A ribbon is 45 inches long. You cut off 18 inches. How long is it now?' Draw a ruler picture and write 45 – 18 = ☐. Solve two more.
days.en: Reflexive pronouns: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves. Fill in 'I made it ___.' and 'We cleaned up ___.' Your child makes up two more.

days.ma: Jump contest: each family member does a standing jump and you measure it in inches or centimeters. Who jumped farthest? How much farther than the shortest jump?
days.en: Your child retells a favorite story aloud from 'Once upon a time' to how the problem was solved, then retells it again changing only the ending.

days.ma: Friday check: show 35 + 20 on a number line; a 62 cm ribbon has 25 cm cut off – how much is left? A desk is 36 inches and a shelf is 52 inches – how much longer is the shelf?
days.en: Dictation: 'I was unhappy, so I had to redo it myself.' and 'Please reread the story and retell it.' Check the prefixes and the reflexive pronoun.

weeks.title: Line plots

spell.rule: Suffixes -ful (full of), -less (without) and -ly (in that way): helpful, careless, quickly

weeks.read: An audiobook or read-aloud from your library's free app or a library visit, then a book on the same topic.

days.ma: Measure 8 pencils or crayons to the nearest inch and write each length in a list.
days.en: Listen to a short audio story or read-aloud. Your child retells the key details, then asks you a question about something they didn't understand.

days.ma: Make a line plot: draw a number line from 1 to 8 inches. Put an X above the right number for each pencil. Add a title and label the inches.
days.en: Suffixes: add -ful, -less or -ly to help, care, hope, fear, sad, quick and slow. Explain the meanings (careful = full of care, careless = without care).

days.ma: Repeated measures: every family member measures the same spoon to the nearest centimeter. Show the results on a line plot. Why might the measurements differ?
days.en: Interview: your child asks a grandparent or neighbor (by phone or in person) three questions about when they were seven, then one follow-up question about an answer.

days.ma: Read the pencil line plot: Which length was most common? How many were longer than 5 inches? What is the difference between the longest and shortest?
days.en: Report back: your child tells the family the three most interesting things from the interview in complete sentences, using adjectives and adverbs, e.g. 'She walked to school happily.'

days.ma: Friday check: measure 5 toys to the nearest inch, make a line plot and answer two questions about it.
days.en: Dictation: 'Be careful and walk slowly.' and 'The fearless cat was very helpful.' Check the suffixes.

weeks.title: Consolidation: time and measurement

spell.rule: Review: oo, ew, ue; soft c and g; doubling and dropping e; prefixes un- and re-; suffixes -ful, -less and -ly

weeks.read: Re-read the research books on your animal and choose favorite pages to share.

days.ma: Time review: you call out five times (6:35, 11:50, 1:15 …) and your child sets them on the paper clock. Then they read three real clocks and add a.m. or p.m.
days.en: Revise the animal report: read it aloud and add one more fact, a better opening or a fun closing. Check two spellings in a dictionary or word list.

days.ma: Measure two shoes in inches and in centimeters. Write how much longer one is in each unit, and why the cm numbers are bigger.
days.en: Make a poster or slide for the report with a title, three labeled pictures and a caption under each.

days.ma: Length word problem: 'A string is 70 cm. Another is 28 cm shorter. How long is it?' Show it on a number line, then your child makes up another.
days.en: Presentation practice: your child presents the report, speaking loudly enough, looking at the audience and using complete sentences.

days.ma: Estimate, then measure, six kitchen items to the nearest inch. Make a line plot of the measurements and say what it shows.
days.en: Record the presentation as audio or video on a phone. Watch it together and name one thing done well and one thing to improve.

days.ma: Friday check: read four clocks to 5 minutes with a.m. or p.m.; measure a book in inches and in cm; solve a length word problem; add an item to the line plot.
days.en: Dictation: 'We were running to school in the city.' and 'Retell the story quickly and carefully.' Then your child presents the report to the family.

weeks.title: Picture graphs and bar graphs

spell.rule: Silent letters: kn (know), wr (write) and mb (lamb)

weeks.read: A story where characters show strong feelings – collect the exact words the author uses for feelings and actions.

days.ma: Survey: ask family and friends (in person or by phone) to choose their favorite fruit from four choices. Tally the answers.
days.en: Read a story and collect feeling words. Rank close ones: glad, happy, thrilled; annoyed, mad, furious. Which word fits the main character best at the end?

days.ma: Picture graph: draw one small picture for each vote, in a row for each fruit. Add a title and label every row.
days.en: Shades of meaning: toss, throw, hurl; look, peek, stare. Act each one out, then use the strongest word in each set in a sentence.

days.ma: Bar graph: turn the same data into a bar graph on paper with grid lines you draw, counting up by 1s. Label both sides and add a title.
days.en: Silent letters: write knee, knot, knew, wrong, wrap, wrist, lamb and climb. Your child crosses out the silent letter in each and reads them aloud.

days.ma: Ask questions: 'How many more chose apples than bananas? How many voted in all? If 3 more chose grapes, which would win?' Your child makes up two questions for you.
days.en: Your child writes about a time they had a big feeling, using strong verbs, feeling words and time words (first, after that, at the end) to show how the feeling changed.

days.ma: Friday check: from a four-category bar graph you draw, find the total, how many more, how many fewer and two categories put together.
days.en: Dictation: 'I knew the answer was wrong.' and 'Climb up and wrap the knot.' Then your child reads the feelings story aloud.

weeks.title: Adding within 1,000

spell.rule: Comparing words with -er and -est (taller, tallest); double the last letter after a short vowel (bigger) and change y to i (happiest)

weeks.read: A chapter book read aloud together over several weeks, a few pages each night.

days.ma: Model it: draw 243 + 135 as hundred squares, ten sticks and ones dots. Add hundreds, tens and ones: 300 + 70 + 8 = 378. Then do 412 + 256.
days.en: Start a chapter book. After the first chapter, your child describes the main character and the setting in complete sentences.

days.ma: Regroup ones: 358 + 127. 8 + 7 = 15 ones, which is 1 ten and 5 ones. Show the trade in a drawing, then write it in columns. Do 246 + 538.
days.en: Build a sentence: start with 'The dog ran.' Add an adjective (The big dog ran.), an adverb (ran fast) and a place (to the park). Then rearrange: 'To the park the big dog ran fast.'

days.ma: Regroup tens: 265 + 182. 6 + 8 = 14 tens, which is 1 hundred and 4 tens. Show it with drawings, then do 374 + 251.
days.en: Compound sentences: join pairs of sentences with and, but or so – 'It rained. We stayed inside.' becomes 'It rained, so we stayed inside.' Do three more.

days.ma: Explain it: solve 199 + 245 by moving 1 over to make 200 + 244. Your child explains why the total doesn't change, then tries 398 + 127.
days.en: Edit an earlier piece of writing: expand two short sentences with describing words and join two others with and or but.

days.ma: Friday check: 324 + 152; 467 + 218; 539 + 286; 600 + 199. Your child explains one using hundreds, tens and ones.
days.en: Dictation: 'The tallest tree was bigger than the house.' and 'My dog is faster, but yours is happier.' Check the -er and -est endings and the comma before but.

weeks.title: Subtracting within 1,000

spell.rule: Irregular plurals that don't just add -s (foot → feet, mouse → mice, child → children)

weeks.read: A science book about plants or seeds, to go with a week-long growing experiment.

days.ma: Model subtraction: draw 586 and cross out 2 hundreds, 4 tens and 3 ones to find 586 – 243 = 343. Then do 759 – 425.
days.en: Start a science observation: put a few dried beans on a damp paper towel in a clear bag or jar by a window. Your child draws and writes what they look like on day 1.

days.ma: Break a ten: 452 – 127. You can't take 7 from 2, so trade 1 ten for 10 ones (4 hundreds, 4 tens, 12 ones). Do 563 – 238.
days.en: Irregular plurals: write foot, tooth, mouse, goose, child, man, woman, fish, sheep and leaf. Your child writes the plural of each and uses three in one silly sentence.

days.ma: Break a hundred: 534 – 172. Trade 1 hundred for 10 tens so you can take 7 tens. Draw it, then write it in columns. Do 618 – 354.
days.en: Read about how seeds grow. Your child explains the steps (seed, root, sprout, leaves) and how one leads to the next, and works out the meaning of two science words.

days.ma: 10 and 100 less: 640 – 10, 640 – 100, 503 – 10, 1,000 – 100. Then check a subtraction by adding: 452 – 127 = 325, so 325 + 127 should equal 452.
days.en: Observation log: draw and write about the beans again. Measure any root in centimeters. What has changed since Monday?

days.ma: Friday check: 785 – 342, 621 – 315, 704 – 260, 900 – 100. Check one by adding and explain one trade.
days.en: Dictation: 'The children saw three mice and some geese.' and 'Brush your teeth and wash your feet.' Then your child writes a final observation sentence for the bean log.

weeks.title: Adding and subtracting within 1,000: zeros and word problems

spell.rule: The aw sound spelled aw, au and al (saw, sauce, walk)

weeks.read: A children's dictionary or picture dictionary, plus any nonfiction book your child chooses.

days.ma: Across zeros: 400 – 136. Trade 1 hundred for 10 tens, then 1 ten for 10 ones. Draw it, then try 302 – 158.
days.en: Dictionary skills: find words by the first letter, then the second letter. Look up draw, paw and sauce, read the meaning and use each in a sentence.

days.ma: Count up instead: 500 – 268. Jump 2 to 270, 30 to 300 and 200 to 500, so the answer is 232. Try 700 – 445.
days.en: Words with two meanings: bat, bark, ring, light, fall. Your child draws two meanings for two words, then uses the sentence to decide which fits: 'The dog will bark.'

days.ma: Big number problems: 'A school has 345 students. 128 go on a trip. How many stay?' and 'A library had 486 books and got 237 more. How many now?' Write equations with ☐.
days.en: aw, au or al? Sort saw, draw, paw, yawn, haul, sauce, walk and talk. Notice aw often comes at the end, au in the middle. Check two in a dictionary.

days.ma: Missing middle: 258 + ☐ = 500. Solve by counting up, then your child makes up a word problem that matches it.
days.en: Read a nonfiction page aloud three times for smoothness, going back over any part that didn't make sense, then answer three who, what or where questions about it.

days.ma: Friday check: 600 – 247, 405 – 189, 356 + 478 and a word problem with three-digit numbers. Check the subtractions by adding.
days.en: Dictation: 'I saw the cat walk and yawn.' and 'We also caught the ball and talked.' Your child checks one spelling in a dictionary.

weeks.title: Shapes: triangles to hexagons, and cubes

spell.rule: Two-syllable words where the first syllable ends in a long vowel (o-pen, pa-per, ti-ger)

weeks.read: Poetry for April's poetry month – shape poems, rhyming poems and silly poems.

days.ma: Shape hunt: find triangles, quadrilaterals (4 sides), pentagons and hexagons at home or in pictures. Count the sides and angles of each.
days.en: Read three poems. Clap the rhythm, then find rhyming words and repeated lines. Talk about how the sounds make each poem funny or calm.

days.ma: Draw from clues: 'a shape with 3 angles', 'a shape with 5 sides', 'a quadrilateral that isn't a square', 'a hexagon'. Use a ruler for straight sides.
days.en: Clap o-pen, pa-per, mu-sic, ti-ger, ro-bot, ba-by, pi-lot and e-ven. Notice that the first syllable ends with a long vowel. Read them quickly.

days.ma: Cube study: find a cube shape (a square box or an ice cube). Count its faces (6), edges (12) and corners (8). Are all the faces the same shape?
days.en: Shape poem: draw an outline (a sun, a leaf) and write describing words around the edge. Choose rich words such as sparkling, golden and sizzling.

days.ma: Build shapes flat on the table with toothpicks or cotton swabs: a triangle, a square, a pentagon and a hexagon. How many sticks for each? What do you notice?
days.en: Record your child reading their poem and a favorite poem aloud with expression. Listen back and add a drawing to go with each.

days.ma: Friday check: draw a pentagon, a hexagon and two different quadrilaterals. How many faces does a cube have? Name a shape with 3 angles.
days.en: Dictation: 'The tiger can open the paper.' and 'The baby likes music, but is it enough?' Then share the recorded poems with family.

weeks.title: Equal groups and arrays

spell.rule: R-controlled ear, eer, air and are (hear, deer, chair, share)

weeks.read: Folktales from around the world – a different country each day.

days.ma: Arrays: arrange pasta or coins in 3 rows of 4 and write 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Then make 2 rows of 5 and 5 rows of 5 and write the addition for each.
days.en: Read a folktale from another country. Your child retells it and states the lesson. How is it like a fable you read in the fall?

days.ma: Array hunt: egg cartons, muffin pans, window panes, buttons on a remote. Your child draws three and writes the repeated addition for each.
days.en: Points of view: find two characters who disagree. Your child reads their lines in two different voices, then explains what each character wants.

days.ma: Rows and columns: draw 4 rows of 3 dots. Add by rows (3 + 3 + 3 + 3) and by columns (4 + 4 + 4). Same total!
days.en: Sort hear, near, deer, cheer, care, share, hair and chair by spelling. Then write a sentence each for where and their.

days.ma: Two-row arrays: make arrays with 2 rows for 6, 8 and 10 – even numbers fill 2 equal rows. Try 7 and 9: what happens?
days.en: Retell the folktale as if you were a different character. How does the story change? How did the main character respond to the challenge?

days.ma: Friday check: draw 3 rows of 5 and write the addition; draw 4 rows of 4; draw 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 as an array; can 9 make 2 equal rows?
days.en: Dictation: 'Where did the deer go?' and 'Their chair is near the stairs.' Then your child retells the week's favorite folktale.

weeks.title: Consolidation: data, three-digit numbers, shapes and arrays

spell.rule: Review: two-syllable long vowels, ear/eer/air/are, silent letters, -er and -est, irregular plurals, aw/au/al

weeks.read: A favorite picture book from the year – re-read it to write a book review.

days.ma: Data review: count four kinds of things in the toy box or pantry, make a bar graph and ask each other three questions about it.
days.en: Book review plan: your child picks a favorite book of the year and lists their opinion and three reasons. Look at the illustrations for extra evidence.

days.ma: Three-digit review: 467 + 285 and 803 – 357. Draw one, write the other in columns and check the subtraction by adding.
days.en: Write the review: name the book and author, state the opinion, give reasons joined with because and also, and end with a concluding sentence.

days.ma: Shapes and arrays: draw a hexagon, a pentagon and 4 rows of 3 dots. Write the repeated addition for the array.
days.en: Edit with a checklist: capitals at the start and for names and places, end punctuation, apostrophes in contractions, and spellings checked in a dictionary.

days.ma: Odd, even and arrays: 'Can 14 chairs make 2 equal rows? 3 equal rows?' Draw to check, then try 12 and 15.
days.en: Spelling review game: you say a word; your child writes it and names the pattern. Add any tricky ones to a personal word list.

days.ma: Friday check: a bar graph question, 356 + 278, 702 – 465, name a 5-sided shape, write an array as addition, odd or even for 19.
days.en: Dictation: 'The children knew their paper was on the chair.' and 'Is the tiger the biggest cat?' Then your child reads the review to a family member.

weeks.title: Rectangles split into rows and columns

spell.rule: More contractions (won't, they're, let's) and possessives with 's (the dog's bowl)

weeks.read: A nonfiction book about animal life cycles – frogs, butterflies or chickens.

days.ma: Grid a rectangle: draw a rectangle and use a ruler to split it into 3 rows and 4 columns of same-size squares. Count the squares: 12.
days.en: Read about a life cycle. Your child explains each stage and how one leads to the next, using the diagram to help.

days.ma: Fold and count: fold a sheet of paper in half, then in half again, then once more. Open it: how many rectangles? Count them by rows.
days.en: Topic words: find life-cycle words (larva, hatch, tadpole, cocoon). Use the sentence, a picture or the glossary to explain each one.

days.ma: Count squares on a waffle, a window grid or a tiled floor by adding the rows. Then check by adding the columns.
days.en: Possessive or contraction? 'The dog's bowl' (belongs to the dog) versus 'The dog's hungry' (the dog is). Your child writes two of each and checks the apostrophes.

days.ma: Rectangles of 12: draw every rectangle you can make from 12 squares (1 by 12, 2 by 6, 3 by 4). Write the addition for each.
days.en: Write an all-about page on one life cycle: a heading, a fact for each of four stages, a labeled diagram and a closing sentence.

days.ma: Friday check: draw a rectangle with 2 rows and 5 columns of squares and count them; how many squares in 4 rows of 3? Draw a rectangle made of 9 squares.
days.en: Dictation: 'Let's look at the frog's eggs.' and 'They're sure the eggs won't hatch today.' Check the apostrophes.

weeks.title: Halves, thirds and fourths

spell.rule: Irregular past tense verbs (sit → sat, hide → hid, tell → told)

weeks.read: Picture books about family trips, celebrations or special days.

days.ma: Fold to share: trace a plate to make paper circles and cut out paper rectangles. Fold them into halves, thirds and fourths and label the parts 'one half', 'a third of', 'a fourth of'.
days.en: Past tense: change sit, hide, tell, run, come, go, give, take, keep and feel into the past. Your child tells you about yesterday using four of them.

days.ma: Fair shares: cut a sandwich or tortilla into 2, 3 and 4 equal parts. Describe each whole as two halves, three thirds or four fourths.
days.en: Plan a story about a special day: draw four boxes (first, next, then, last) with one detail each about actions, thoughts and feelings.

days.ma: Different shapes, equal shares: cut a paper square into fourths two ways (four small squares and four strips). Are the shares equal? Cut and match to prove it.
days.en: Write the special day story from the plan using past tense verbs, time words and a closing sentence about how the day ended.

days.ma: Equal or not? Draw shapes split into equal and unequal parts. Your child sorts them and explains why some parts are not halves or thirds.
days.en: Your child tells the special day story aloud without reading it, with facts and descriptive details. Each listener asks one question.

days.ma: Friday check: shade one half of a circle, a third of a rectangle and a fourth of a square. How many fourths make a whole? Is a given split equal?
days.en: Dictation: 'We went to the park and sat by the lake.' and 'She hid the gift and told no one.' Then your child reads the finished story.

weeks.title: Revisit: place value and comparing to 1,000

spell.rule: Two-syllable words ending in -le; double the consonant after a short vowel (lit-tle, bub-ble)

weeks.read: Two nonfiction books or articles on the same topic, such as bees or volcanoes.

days.ma: Number of the day: pick 507. Write it in words and expanded form, draw it, and say 10 more, 10 less, 100 more and 100 less. Repeat with a number your child picks.
days.en: Read the first text. What is the author's purpose – to answer a question, explain or describe? Your child finds a sentence that shows it.

days.ma: Ordering: write eight three-digit numbers, order them from least to greatest, then write three comparisons using <, > and =.
days.en: Find one point the author makes ('Bees are important') and the reasons given for it. Your child says whether the reasons were convincing.
Read the second text on the same topic. Chart the most important points in each and circle the points both texts share.

days.ma: Place value riddles: 'I have 6 hundreds, no tens and 4 ones.' 'I am 100 more than 299.' 'I have 4 hundreds and 13 tens.' Your child writes two riddles for you.
days.en: -le words: clap the syllables in table, apple, little, puzzle, candle, bubble, purple and simple. Notice the double consonant after a short vowel.

days.ma: Friday check: write 846 in expanded form and in words; 100 less than 312; compare 569 and 596; count by 5s from 980 to 1,000.
days.en: Dictation: 'The little apple was purple.' and 'This puzzle is simple but different.' Then your child explains a key point; you ask a question and they answer it.

weeks.title: Review: addition and subtraction

spell.rule: Review fall patterns: short and long vowels, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels and diphthongs

weeks.read: A favorite chapter book to finish, plus a fairy tale and a different version of it.

days.ma: Fact fluency: 30 mixed facts within 20 in 3 minutes. Compare with how it went in the fall and circle any facts that still need practice.
days.en: Read a fairy tale and answer who, what, where, when, why and how questions. Draw a beginning, middle and end strip.

days.ma: Within 100: 67 + 28, 83 – 45 and 39 + 26 + 15 + 12. Show one on a number line.
days.en: Read another version of the same tale, or ask a grandparent how they heard it. Compare the characters, settings and endings in a chart.

days.ma: Within 1,000: 485 + 367 and 703 – 258. Your child explains each step aloud.
days.en: Spelling review: spell the ten words aloud and in writing, then sort them by pattern.

days.ma: Problem solving: one two-step problem within 100 and one with three-digit numbers. Your child chooses a bar drawing or number line for each.
days.en: Fluency: read a page of the chapter book three times for smooth, expressive reading and record the last reading.

days.ma: Friday check: ten facts, two problems within 100, two within 1,000 and one word problem with ☐.
days.en: Dictation: 'A star was bright in the night sky.' and 'The bird sat on the toy drum.' Then your child retells the fairy tale.

weeks.title: Review: measurement, time, money, data and shapes

spell.rule: Review winter and spring patterns: prefixes, suffixes, contractions, silent letters, soft c and g

weeks.read: A nonfiction book on a summer topic – the beach, insects or camping.

days.ma: Time and money: show 4:25 p.m. on the clock; count 3 quarters, 2 dimes and 1 nickel; 'You have $1. A snack costs 65¢. How much is left?'
days.en: Read a summer nonfiction book. Your child works out the meaning of three new words using the sentence, the glossary or a dictionary.

days.ma: Estimate, then measure, four items in inches, feet, centimeters or meters. Show the inch lengths on a line plot.
days.en: Grammar review: your child writes one sentence each with a collective noun, an irregular plural, a reflexive pronoun, an irregular past tense verb and an adverb.

days.ma: Shapes and shares: draw a hexagon; split a rectangle into 3 rows and 3 columns; shade a third of a circle and a half of a square.
days.en: Word review: sort un-, re-, -ful and -less words and put warm, hot and boiling in order. Use three of them in sentences.

days.ma: Survey the family's favorite summer activity (four choices), draw a bar graph and write two compare questions.
days.en: Write an informative paragraph on a summer topic: an opening, three facts and a closing. Revise one sentence to make it clearer.

days.ma: Friday check: a clock to 5 minutes, a money problem, a length difference, a bar graph question, naming a shape and an equal-shares drawing.
days.en: Dictation: 'I can't refill the cup quickly.' and 'They're careful in the city.' Check the prefixes, suffixes and apostrophes.

weeks.title: Fun project: plan a family summer fair

spell.rule: Spelling celebration: choose ten favorite words from this year's lists and make a personal dictionary page

weeks.read: Your child's choice – favorite books from the year to re-read and recommend.

days.ma: Plan a backyard or living-room fair with four game stations. Make a schedule with start times to 5 minutes (2:00 p.m., 2:15 p.m., 2:35 p.m. …).
days.en: Hold a planning meeting: everyone suggests game ideas, takes turns speaking and builds on others' ideas. Your child writes the final list.

days.ma: Price board: give each game and snack a price in cents (25¢, 40¢ …). Your child makes the price board and works out the cost of playing all four games.
days.en: Opinion poster for the best game: 'You should play … because … Also …' with a big title and a drawing.

days.ma: Set up the stations: mark a beanbag or sock toss line 6 feet away and a hopping lane 3 meters long with a tape measure and string.
days.en: Make an invitation on a computer or by hand with the day, time and place. If it is a note to a neighbor, use commas after the greeting and closing.

days.ma: Run the fair: family members pay with real coins, your child gives change and keeps a tally of how many times each game is played.
days.en: Research one game children play in another country, using a library book or a children's website with an adult. Write its rules in three steps and add it to the fair.

days.ma: Friday check: make a bar graph of plays per game; how many plays in all? Which game was most popular? Add the money taken at the four stations.
days.en: Celebrate: your child records a short audio or video 'news report' about the fair, then tells the family what they learned this year and what they look forward to in Grade 3.
